title: Best Game So Far!! | Mastering the Alapin Sicilian | GM Naroditsky's Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: We open d4, Black replies d5. In queen's-pawn openings like the London this often leads to a queen b3 versus b6 standoff.
We develop the bishop to f4 — the London System.
Black develops the knight to f6 and we support with e3.
We develop the knight to f3.
We buttress with c3, and Black brings the knight to c6.
We complete the setup with the knight to d2.
Black plays the standard queen to b6, eyeing b2.
We meet it with the queen to b3 — the classic standoff, where neither side wants to be the one to capture, even though it damages a pawn structure.

Black trades and we recapture with the a-pawn — not the knight — opening the a-file and keeping a serious edge. The lesson: pawn structure is subservient to piece placement and activity; the doubled b-pawns are a small price for the open file and better pieces.

Two big themes surface here. First, the power of a knight or bishop planted on d6 (or d3) when the opponent's queenside is undeveloped — such a piece can paralyse a whole flank, and it's devastating when a back-rank bishop has no way out. Second, prophylactic thinking: always ask what your opponent WANTS and prevent it — not just concrete threats but improving ideas like ...e6, worth stopping even though it wins nothing, because it frees the opponent's game.

And a London reflex worth keeping: meeting a bishop to d6 with the bishop to g3, trading on your own terms — here recapturing toward the centre to open the file, the same principle applied to a different file.
